speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, October 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-78, an Act to amend the Governor General's Act, the Governor General's Retiring Annuity Act, the Salaries Act and the Judges Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, this is principally a Bill to increase judges' salaries, as well as those of the Governor General and Lieutenant-Governors. It refers as well to pensions along with salaries. What I want to speak about, however, is the salaries of judges. As the Government itself notes, notwithstanding this Bill it has put forward, there is the problem of spending restraint.
What we have here is a proposed raise in salaries for the judges retroactive to April 1 of this year. For example, the chief Justice of the Supreme Court is now receiving $117,000 annually with a cost of living adjustment capped at 7 per cent. His salary goes up by 7 per cent or the cost of living each year, whichever is less. At present inflation is less than 7 per cent but it will go up by 3 per cent or 4 per cent next year no doubt. However, this Bill proposes that his salary be increased to $135,000 retroactive to April 1, and I understand the cost of living increase would continue. The salaries of other judges of the court go up from $108,400 to $124,000, again retroactive to April 1. In the Superior Court, the Chief Justice now gets $101,800 and that will be increased to $113,900. Puisne judges will have an increase to $105,000. The chief judge of a district or county court will receive $108,900 and the salaries of other judges, now at $86,900, will increase to $100,000. In addition there is what is called the representation allowance. Judges are sometimes called upon to act in a public way and travel, and most of them are allowed up to $5,000 for representation costs. That will now be doubled to $10,000.
There are, Mr. Speaker, somewhere between 700 and 800 judges covered by this Bill. That, of course, is not a very large number in a country of 25 million so it can be argued that the money involved is not a great amount. It is not like the $1 billion being paid to bail out the banks. It is not like the $1
billion being given to the oil companies. However, there is a principle involved, that of restraint. These increases amount to 12 per cent or 15 per cent. That is a remarkably large increase compared to what almost every other public servant receives. It is a remarkably large increase compared to what ordinary wage earners and professional people in private employment receive. It is a shockingly large increase when compared with what is happening to people on mother's allowance.
Now, we are told that there is a problem. The judges have a problem which requires special consideration. They have a cash flow problem. I understand they need to spend more than they receive and therefore they have a cash flow problem. This problem is very easy to understand. A great many people in the country have the same problem. For example, there are millions of mothers in this land, whose income is only a small fraction of that of the judges, who have cash flow problems. There are thousands of mothers in my riding of Spadina who receive the family allowance and have cash flow problems. They have it every day when they go to the grocery store and every month when they pay the rent. Of course they are not the only ones, but I mention them particularly because the Government has decided that this country is so poor that it must reduce the effective income that mothers receive from mother's allowance by 3 per cent every year.
[DOT] (i HO)
There are others who are affected less directly. For example, many people need legal aid but the budgets for legal aid offices are being cut back or, at best, frozen rather than increased in accordance with the cash flow problems of the lawyers and other workers in those legal aid offices. They would like a little more money to pay the higher prices because they have a cash flow problem. Of course, that does not fall directly under federal jurisdiction, but some of the problems that require people to use legal aid are under federal jurisdiction.
For example, people come to my office who have immigration problems with the federal Government. They may be getting a raw deal through a mistake or perhaps through a bias in the administration. They may need the services of a lawyer, but very often new immigrants cannot afford that and must go to legal aid. There they run into these people with the cash flow problems. Both the legal aid clinics and the people who work there have that problem and it makes it difficult for them to give service to the people who need legal aid in order to argue their case before the immigration commission.
People who have trouble with unemployment insurance have difficulty getting legal aid because of the cash flow problem of the legal aid clinic. The same applies to pensioners. It occasionally happens that a pensioner cannot get his or her prob-

lem resolved, even with the help of an MP or another helpful person on a voluntary basis, and must get a lawyer. Once again they run into a cash flow problem.
Now that the grape boycott has been launched in Parliament today there will be some difficulties between boycotters and stores. There may be some controversies arising out of that and there may be some people who will need legal aid to defend themselves against an over-hasty charge laid by the police who are trying to keep order on the picket line. They will come to the legal aid clinics and find that there is a cash flow problem.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that just about everyone of whom I have heard has a cash flow problem. I do not know whether the President of the Bank of Montreal has a personal cash flow problem because he has not told me, but the people who come to my office have cash flow problems and most of them receive only a quarter or an eighth of the income that judges now receive. Therefore, I think that their cash flow problems are much more serious than those of the judges.
My Party and I feel that this is not the right time to give the judges such a big raise. It may be that in times of affluence we can give them a little more, but at this time of restraint when we are cutting back family allowances and so many of the programs which help ordinary working people, all of whom have cash flow problems, it is not right to be raising the pay of judges by the astonishing amount of 12 or 15 per cent retroactive for nearly a whole year. For instance, if the Government were persuaded by the public of Canada to withdraw its legislation that will reduce the family allowance that is available to mothers, as it wisely did in June with respect to pensions, and if it withdrew other forms of taxation, such as increased sales tax, which bears so heavily on working people, I think there would be a better environment and a better public attitude within which to increase the judges' pay by this or some other amount. However, I suggest it would seem monstrously unfair to do so at this time.
While I am not a lawyer, I would suggest that it seems unjust to give an extra large increase to people who already have more while we are taking away from the people who already have less. We know that there is a saying in the gospels that, "To those that have shall be given and from those that have not shall be taken away" but whatever that means, that was meant to be the action of God, not the action of this Parliament. On the basis of our Charter, we certainly cannot find any justification for taking money away from mothers on family allowances and giving it to judges who already earn five or even ten times as much.
If the Government wished to amend this Bill so that the judges' salaries would increase according to the cost of living minus 3 per cent, I and I believe other Mmeber of my Party would be willing to take a very fresh look at it. I am not sure that the cost of living or Consumer Price Index will be this year perhaps 3.5 per cent, but if that is the case the judges would receive the same increase as mothers, that is, 0.5 per
cent. I suggest that most people would consider that to be reasonably fair. While it may be a perfect solution for mothers or judges, most people would agree that it would be fair.
Furthermore, since judges are in the business of justice, I hope even they would suggest that it would be a just decision, especially since some of the judges are women and perhaps mothers. I hope even they would suggest to the Government that a just compromise would be that judges' pay not be increased as proposed but rise each year by an amount equal to the Consumer Price Index minus 3 per cent so long as that is the formula being applied to the mothers of Canada.

subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AND RELATED ACTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-75, An Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act and to amend the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, the Maritime Code Act and the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendments which are contained in Bill C-75 which I am introducing today will reaffirm the Canada Shipping Act as the principal Act of Parliament dealing with safety of shipping, the preservation of life at sea and the protection of the marine environment in Canadian waters and fishing zones. The last time major amendments were made to the Canada Shipping Act was in 1971. These dealt specifically with pollution from ships. The Liberal Government of the day was jolted into taking stopgap measures by the tragic events surrounding the break up of the Arrow. As all Hon. Members will know, there is considerable demand for and widespread interest in these amendments by all sectors of the marine industry and the maritime bar. For example, there is an immediate requirement for amendments to the Canada Shipping Act to enhance safety at sea; to enable Canada to deal more effectively with matters associated with marine pollution; to allow for the Government to consider charging for certain Coast Guard services; and to give effect to important
October 15, 1985

international marine conventions, such as the 1978 Protocol to the Safety of Life at Sea Convention, the Convention of Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers and the Convention for Prevention of Pollution from Ships. Most Hon. Members will be aware that Canada has been unable to ratify and hence become a party to these conventions because of not having the necessary enabling legislation.
In layman's terms, apart from those amendments of an administrative nature, what I am proposing today relates principally to health, safety, recovery of costs and financial protection for individuals, all of which are of concern to everyone associated with maritime transportation and trade in Canada. As well, the two items announced last year as part of the Government's restraint program are included in this legislation.
First, in order to avoid unnecessary duplication of ship inspections, the amendments will enable the delegation of routine inspection of ships to classification societies. This of course will be done in accordance with our regulations. Safety equipment will continue to be inspected by the Coast Guard. This will amount to a cost saving of some $200,000 annually.
Second, amendments are also included which would permit the option of transferring the provisions of port warden services to the private sector. If this option is exercised, cargoes will continue to be loaded and inspected in accordance with the regulations made under the Act, but the actual inspections would be carried out by private sector surveyors.
Another very important provision provides for the enabling authority for the recovery of certain Coast Guard expenses for services such as ice-breaking, escort services and aids to navigation.
Perhaps, in introducing this provision, it is necessary to take a few minutes to elaborate on the services which I have mentioned. I am sure Hon. Members on both sides of the House may be somewhat amazed at the depth and breadth of Coast Guard activities presently provided at virtually no charge to the maritime community. The Coast Guard provides a multiplicity of services to the marine sector. These include a sophisticated system of aids to navigation; radio aids and maintenance of ship channels; ship movement systems, such as the vessel traffic services and a network of radio stations; and ice-breaking services for commercial shipping, flood control and support of arctic operations. The Coast Guard is the principal marine component for search and rescue operations, with particular emphasis upon the safety of pleasure craft through education on boating safety and regulatory activities which encompass the safety of shipping, including the examination and certification of personnel, the licensing and registration of vessels, and the inspection of ships and their cargoes. Additionally, the Coast Guard deals with pollution clean-up from marine-related sources and other marine emergencies.
The Coast Guard operates from bases in five regions across Canada. In support of its functions, it deploys a fleet of 86
Canada Shipping Act
vessels ranging from major ice-breakers to shore-based search and rescue lifeboats, some 34 helicopters, four hovercraft and one aircraft, plus a number of inshore rescue boats and various sized work boats.
The total operating and capital costs, including administrative costs, in the 1985-86 fiscal year for the Coast Guard are in the region of $824 million. This includes costs of $368 million for aids to navigation; $74 million for ship movement systems and services; $177 million for ice-breaking, Arctic and ship support services; $62 million for marine search and rescue; $37 million for regulatory activities including marine emergencies; and $72 million for public ports and harbours.
I would like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Coast Guard is a vital component of the marine transportation system, contributing to the safe and expeditious movement of shipping and, most important, the safety of life at sea.
I would like to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that the introduction of charges for certain Coast Guard services and the concept of privatizing the port warden services would only proceed after consultation with interested parties in the public and private sectors. I will be directing my Department to establish a consultative committee, mandated to meet with groups across the country, including shipowners and their representatives; unions, shippers and shipper-groups, fishermen and their associations, and other representatives of the marine industry and users of the marine infrastructure.
Let me turn now to other details of the Bill. The amendments will provide for clear authority for vessel traffic zones and the procedures to be followed by ships in or about to enter such zones. The Bill also provides for the designation of marine traffic administrators and delineates the circumstances under which they may issue directions to ships in Canadian waters.
I would emphasize here that there is no intention to undermine or take away the authority of masters or pilots but instead, to work with these professionals to enhance the safety and integrity of the existing system.
There would be no additional financial expenditures, public or private, associated with vessel traffic services, as these systems are already in place.
Experience in administering Part XX, the pollution section of the existing Act, which was prepared on an urgent basis as a sequel to the Arrow disaster of 1970, has revealed serious faults and omissions, and these amendments aim to correct those faults and omissions. Further, through a lack of enabling legislation, Canada has been unable to implement and obtain the advantage of the assured compensation provided by two international conventions; the 1969 International Convention on Civil Liability for Oil Pollution Damage, and the 1971 International Convention on the Establishment of an International Fund for Compensation for Oil Pollution Damage.
These amendments, Mr. Speaker, therefore provide not only improvements in pollution prevention from ships and the

October 15, 1985
Canada Shipping Act
arrangements for clean-up, but also a greatly improved scheme of liability and compensation for the victims of oil pollution damage.
For instance, if a 60,000-ton laden tanker importing crude into Canada experienced a spill today, the owner of that ship would be required to make approximately $8.7 million available to pay compensation for pollution damage; that is to say, the maximum amount available would be $8.7 million, plus any moneys that there might be in the maritime pollution claims fund. The balance of that domestic fund is currently approximately $110 million. On the other hand, there would be assured compensation of $60 million from the two aforementioned international conventions and $100 million from the maritime pollution claims fund.
Improvements are to be made to the maritime pollution claims fund, which will be renamed the ship source oil pollution fund, whereby small claimants, such as fishermen and resort owners, will in future be able to claim directly against that fund.
Compensation for a ship other than a laden tanker will be at least $100 million, provided from the Canadian fund.
Within a similar context, Mr. Speaker, the powers of pollution prevention officers to board ships will be modified to conform to the inspection provisions of the International Pollution Convention. They will also be authorized to delineate emergency zones and to control traffic within those zones and, in cases where there is the likelihood of a spill, order any ship to move or to proceed as directed, and also, for purposes of prosecution, to obtain samples of pollutants from ships without first having to obtain a search warrant.
Additionally, to comply with the recommendation of the Auditor General, designated officials will be empowered to enter premises to inspect the books and financial records of contributors to our own domestic oil spill compensation fund.
Included in these amendments providing for discretionary authority for officials, the Board of Steamship Inspection would be able to permit adoption of equivalent standards in respect of such items as the structural strength of ships and equipment or exemption from regulations where this may be deemed desirable or appropriate. The board would also be empowered to prescribe interim standards for the carriage of dangerous goods in bulk for new substances for which standards do not exist and where time does not permit the making of a regulation.
With reference to dangerous goods, Hon. Members may wish to note that the amendments will provide for more effective regulation of the carriage by sea of dangerous goods in bulk by bringing the provisions of the Act into line with the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act. Bulk cargoes will continue to be regulated under the Canada Shipping Act while packaged goods will in future be regulated on a multimodal basis under the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act.
With respect to safety at sea, the amendments will promote safety and more efficient navigation. For instance, they will enable the introduction of new and improved standards for the training and certification of seafarers including, very importantly, special qualifications for service on ships such as oil and chemical tankers and mobile offshore drilling units. I think Hon. Members only have to recall the tragic events of the Ocean Ranger, the Hudson Transport and the Cartiercliffe Hall to understand the importance of this amendment which will enable the adoption of recommendations on safety training, made by these formal investigations. There will be some additional cost to both industry and Government in undertaking this training but this must be balanced against the benefits in terms of safety and environmental protection.
Specifically, the cost of training in respect to seafarers of the industry would be in the magnitude of $24 million over the next five years and for employees on civilian government ships it would be in the magnitude of some $4.8 million over the same five-year period. The cost for employees on government ships will be absorbed by appropriate Departments such as the Departments of Transport, Fisheries and Oceans, National Defence and Public Works, and of course the cost to the private sector will be absorbed by the individual firms. It is far easier to put a dollar figure on the cost of training and prevention than it is to estimate the price we may pay in loss of lives and irretractable damage to the environment if we do not proceed in this area.
With respect to ship integrity, particular standards for the construction and equipment of mobile offshore drilling units and special purpose ships have been adopted internationally. These amendments will enable Canada to implement these standards. As well, the amendments provide for the implementation of the 1978 Protocol on Tanker Safety and the 1974 Safety of Life at Sea Convention regarding such matters as inspections, steering gear, fire protection and navigational equipment.
In addition to the foregoing, there are a number of other amendments relating to dynamically supported craft such as air cushion vehicles, tonnage measurement, abolition of hard labour as a penalty under the Act, restricted application of rules and regulations, the recording of Government ships in the shipping registry and a provision that would enable foreign flag ships to be exempted from the prohibitory provisions of the Act relating to the coasting trade when suitable Canadian ships are not available. This latter provision has been in place since 1973 and is retained as an interim measure for use until such time as a separate coasting trade Act is developed, a point I shall address later in my remarks.
It should be noted that the Bill is drafted to permit the regulation of matters relating to drill ships and structures, their construction and equipment and training and certification of personnel on board while actively engaged in exploration and exploitation on Canada Lands to be regulated under the Canada Oil and Gas Act. At all other times, these vessels will be regulated under the Canada Shipping Act.
October 15, 1985

I am sure Hon. Members would appreciate my referring to other aspects of marine-related legislation mentioned in my recent discussion paper on economic regulatory reform entitled Freedom to Move. The Shipping Conferences Exemption Act, 1979, was extended for a further year by the Government and now expires on March 31, 1986. I am anxious that some of the uncertainty surrouding the future of this subject be dispelled as soon as possible since proposed revisions to the legislation in one form or another have been under discussion for some time now both by the previous Liberal administration and by this Government. I therefore propose to present a revised shipping conferences exemption Bill to Parliament separate from and ahead of revisions to the National Transportation Act with the hope that Parliament will dispose of the subject before the most recent extension to the Shipping Conferences Exemption Act of 1979 expires.
A further item referred to in Freedom to Move that I intend to put before Parliament before the new National Transportation Act is introduced is a Bill concerning amendments to the previously mentioned Coasting Trade Act of Canada. I should explain that coasting trade provisions are now covered under Part XV of the present Canada Shipping Act, and indeed the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act which I am proposing do in fact contain an amendment to Part XV, which is necessary to correct a technical problem which is of some concern. However, the amendment is only there to remove any doubts about the legality of existing practices.
Consistent with Freedom to Move, the new coasting trade Bill will, among other things, extend the jurisdiction to 200 nautical miles or to the limit of the continental shelf, whichever is greater. It will expand the scope of the act to include all commercial marine activities except fishing, yet it will still retain a waiver system to allow foreign flag ships to satisfy temporary requirements.
Last, Freedom to Move made references to the Inland Water Freight Rates Act and the Transport Act. I propose to deal with the future of both of these pieces of legislation when the new National Transportation Act is introduced to Parliament some time early next year.
It is more important at this particular time that the House deal expeditiously with what I am proposing today. As I said earlier, the Canada Shipping Act is the principal Act of Parliament dealing with the safety of shipping, the preservation of life and the protection of the marine environment in Canadian waters and fishing zones. As outlined, it deals with such diverse matters as vessel ownership, tonnage measurement, certification and training of seafarers, construction and equipment of ships, safe navigation, civil liability, cargoes, the prevention of pollution from ships and compensation for the victims of oil pollution damage. Its provisions ensure that all ships entering Canadian waters and using our ports comply with standards that provide a high degree of safety and efficiency.
These amendments, which have taken considerable time to develop, have been widely discussed and generally endorsed by all interest groups including ship owners, shipbuilders and
Canada Shipping Act
repairers, trade unions, the oil industry, fishing interests and other agencies of Government. I believe the Bill goes a long way toward modernizing an outdated piece of legislation and making it responsive to today's needs.
Canada is fortunate to have a solid reputation within the international maritime community. In fact, I am proud to note for Hon. Members that Mr. Bill O'Neil, the President of the St. Lawrence Seaway, was the first Canadian elected as Chairman of the Council of the U.N. International Maritime Organization in 1979. He was subsequently re-elected to this position in both 1981 and 1983.
Let me reiterate to the House that there are approximately 12 major international conventions and codes that Canda cannot effect until these amendments are passed. The maritime community, both at home and abroad, awaits these amendments to bring this legislation governing the seafaring trade into 1986 and beyond. This legislation will re-establish Canada's credibility in the marine sector. I therefore call upon all Hon. Members to give expeditious pasage to this Bill.

subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in looking at this Bill, which is quite an elaborate piece of legislation that cannot be absorbed very quickly, my impression of which 1 would like to speak today is that the Government of Canada is expecting a growing volume of year-round oil tanker shipping in Arctic waters. I will address the subject of the Arctic in the next few minutes. As well, the Minister has given a much broader and more comprehensive perspective to the Bill than the one I will develop.
The reality of the South is one thing and the reality of the North is another. It seems to me that the Minister needs to be sensitized to some of the realities of the North in view of the fact that by amending the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, this Bill spells bad news for northern people and the northern areas of the country from an environmental point of view. I would like to provide the Minister with some background on this. He has referred to the groups with which he has consulted or intends to consult. He did not make a reference, at least I did not hear him make any reference to the native people. I would like to refer him to some documentation of which his Department ought to be aware, beginning with the Lancaster Sound regional study of November of 1983. It is a document which embodies a public review. It consists of public consultation, and I will just put on the record a few selected passages because they seem to be quite relevant to this Bill which will generate growing volumes of year-round tanker shipping in the Arctic. George Eckalook, speaking on behalf of the Resolute Bay Settlement Council, stated:
-the settlement wants Lancaster Sound to stay in its present state and not be touched at all. The people of the settlement want to protect the environment, they want to learn more, to consider the possibility of parks, and to wait for the Nunavut land claims settlement. They are concerned about the possible use of icebreaking ships moving through the Sound during the winter and are frightened by the possible explosion of natural gas being carried by these ships.

October 15, 1985
Canada Shipping Act
Sampson Akpaleapik, a student in grade nine at the Takijualuk School in Pond Inlet, expressed on the same occasion an opinion that, and I quote:
-if there was an oil spill in the Sound the fish would suffocate. The narwhals, seals, and other sea animals would die out. If there was an oil spill, the marine currents would spread the oil rapidly killing the animals that the whales, seals, and walruses eat. Even if there was no oil spill, the noise of the ships' engines would scare the animals away.
Maggie Allooloo, speaking on behalf of the Development Review Committee of the Hamlet Council of Pond Inlet, stated emphatically and I quote:
-the Council does not want development of non-renewable resources at this time. Even with planning, heavy controls, and strict regulations, the Development Review Committee feels that activity associated with non-renewable resource development would grow beyond what the environment and the people could tolerate. The Committee is in favour of option two as outlined in the Green Paper, and after land claims are settled, the final decisions on the National Park in the area could be worked out.
Charlie Inuarak, speaking on behalf of the Baffin Region Inuit Association, reviewed the association's positions with respect to conservation, uncertainty about impacts, and the narrow definition that equates national interest to Canada's energy supply. He stated:
The key question for BRIA is: do we choose to put the Lancaster Sound Region at risk? In response, BRIA contends that if we are serious about the principle of the maintenance of biological productivity and environmental quality, then no hydrocarbon activities should be allowed to proceed in the Lancaster Sound Region.
You can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that the Lancaster Sound would be right smack in the middle of many of these shipping movements if they were to take place. I am sure you, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), have seen the beauty and richness of that ecological body of water and you are aware of how fragile it is and how much it represents one of the last unique resources of this particular quality in the entire globe.
In the same document, a position was taken by the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee, of which, I am sure, the Minister is familiar, as an organization with which he intends to consult or has consulted. The report reads as follows, first:
That the moratorium on exploratory drilling and year round shipping be continued until a satisfactory regional planning process and a northern conversation policy are in place;
Second:
That the establishment of a planning process recognize the political development and land claim initiatives which are now taking place in the Northwest Territories.
And third:
That all immediate decisions regarding Lancaster Sound be made in line with the general principles that CARC developed in 1979.
We have here, Mr. Speaker, an input from North by people who live there are who follow developments such as the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee which really seems to be expressing a viewpoint which is diametrically opposite to the direction in which this Government intends to go. I can only express profound disappointment in the absence so far of consultations with the organizations of the North and also with the Inuit Tapirisats and with the territorial Governments
as well as, perhaps, Environment Canada or the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I believe it is essential, Mr. Speaker, that a thorough consultation, which has not taken place up to now, be part and parcel of the examination of the Bill after second reading so as to allow input from the people in the areas affected and the consideration of lifestyles and cultures which are going to be affected if this Bill goes through and eventually leads to growing volumes of year-round oil and tanker shipping.
There has been a draft Green Paper on Lancaster Sound and the North. There has been Lancaster Sound regional study. There has also been a Green Paper on the Lancaster Sound region 1980-2000. It is basically this Green Paper I would like to be sure the Minister is familiar with. It needs to be examined in the light of the main thrust of this Bill, which is to increase liability and compensation and to destroy the ecology and lifestyle in the North by the tanker traffic which will inevitably lead to serious consequences.
I am told that the Inuit Tapirisats Organization feels very strongly about any activity which would contemplate tanker movement through Lancaster Sound, and that the public hearings so far did determine an attitude which rejected that notion. The Inuit Tapirisats, as an organization and as individuals, would be simply outraged, if, after second reading, consultations had not taken place in committee and a decision made.
I realize that will be a very difficult situation to resolve by the Minister in the application of this Bill if he intends, as it is my assumption he does, to increase the volume of year-round tanker shipping in the Arctic. That will mean that once again we will have imposed our values and our economic goals on a culture which so far has managed to survive under very difficult circumstances and in a very fragile ecological set-up. Basically, this tends to reject our exploitation of the natural resources in the way we do it as a white society. There is a very strong commitment to finding ways of exploiting our renewable resources, but certainly in my experience there is a rejection of the exploitation of oil and gas in a manner which will cause damage to the environment which no amount of compensation can adequately repair. We all know the beauty of Lancaster Sound and I can hardly imagine anyone in his right mind who would want to see any damage caused to that beautiful body of water. It is one of the most striking of its kind in the world, and increasing liability and compensation from present levels to the highest amount any Government could afford is not really coming to grips with the important ecological and cultural question before us, namely whether we want to move into that environment and pollute it. Regardless of the good intentions and the prevention schemes which may be in place, cleaning up marine pollution in the Arctic is virtually impossible once the damage is done. It is difficult to do that even in our climate and latitude, as our experience off the Atlantic coast some 10 years ago has shown. It is virtually impossible to do it in our Arctic areas once the spill has taken place.
October 15, 1985

It is therefore necessary to bring this to the attention of the Minister of Transport and ensure that he has the support of his colleague, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), as well as the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie). He has to ensure that a proposal of this kind also has the full support and understanding of the territorial Governments. Beyond that, the bottom line is that he has to have the support of the native people in the regions affected. My impression is that, by and large, the native communities in the North would reject the notion of a year-round oil tanker route for the reasons I have already identified by way of quotations from the Lancaster Sound Regional Study produced by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Evidently the attitude of people up there is one that rejects any activity which would have the potential to damage permanently the ecology and the environment per se.
I urge the Minister to travel to and consult with the people in communities like Pond Inlet and Tuktoyaktuk and Grise Ford and others in order to see with his own eyes the ecological reality. Standing in the North and looking south gives you a perspective quite different from that of standing here in this House and looking North. I am sure that if he were to do that, he would have profound doubts about the advisability of using this Bill to increase year-round oil tanker traffic.
The reason I raise these questions is that I know the Minister is a democrat, he listens to people and he wants to be fully informed about the implications of any measure he brings to Parliament, not just from the perspective of the industrialized South but from that of the North. My impression is that if we were to tap the oil and gas resources of the North, we could get the support of the native people there if we did it by land, if we were to do it by way of pipelines, which are operated under strict controls, well-regulated and environmentally safe. That is where the thrust has been for some time. But when it comes to the alternative of doing it by sea where the possibility of an accidental spill is increased many, many times, then we are talking a completely different approach. This can only be fully understood if you stand, for example, on a hill in Pond Inlet and look out over Lancaster Sound. This is unique water body, ecologically speaking one of the richest in the world. Then try to envisage a tanker route moving through that part of our Arctic. It is unthinkable. Therefore, I submit that we should be extremely careful in laying the foundations for such an initiative which would have such profound consequences on the lifestyle and ecological riches of our North.
The main thrust of this intervention on my part today is to impress upon the Minister and the Government the absolute necessity of thorough consultations with the native people. It is of the greatest importance that this Bill be explained to them. It is difficult for us to fathom it in all its details here today, and one can only imagine what difficulty it poses to people who live several thousand miles away. It is important that the Bill be understood, because a one-page press release cannot do justice to a Bill which runs some 106 pages and which contains
Canada Shipping Act
a very important chapter on pollution prevention and control and which has politically, I suspect, some profound and longterm implications. Therefore, the Minister of Transport and his Government owe this House as well as the affected communities a thorough explanation as to what the long-term policy of this Government is in relation to year-round oil tanker traffic in Arctic waters. This is the basic policy direction which has to be understood on second reading of Bill C-75.

subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise to speak on Bill C-75, an Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, among others. I do so in my role as my Party's spokesperson for marine activities and, in particular, for the St. Lawrence Seaway. While this Act is basically an effort to bring the marine industry into the twentieth century, I believe it has one serious flaw. Before I get to that, I would like to say that the matters raised by the Government in this Bill are extremely important. I agree with the Minister that we should move them through the House and committee as quickly as possible. However, we may have some difficulty with this one flaw.
Bill C-75 takes the former Government's user-pay philosophy for the St. Lawrence Seaway and expands it into the Conservative Government's philosophy for cost recovery on the remainder of the marine industry in Canada. Clause 4 of this Act gives the Government the power to require that any amount up to 100 per cent of the cost of providing Coast Guard services be passed on to the users. It is important to this debate, Mr. Speaker, that 1 read the clause that I am so concerned about. It reads:
3.1(1) For the purpose of defraying the cost of navigational services provided by the Canadian Coast Guard, the Governor in Council may make regulations respecting charges relating to those services, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, aids to navigation, dredging, vessel traffic services, ice breaking services and escorting services.
(2) Charges may be imposed pursuant to subsection (1) in relation to any ship or vessel, regardless of whether the Canadian Coast Guard actually provides a navigational service to that particular ship or vessel.
Those are fairly broad powers given to the Minister of Transportation (Mr. Mazankowski) and Cabinet. 1 want you to understand, Mr. Speaker, that regardless of my comments and those of my colleagues who will follow me, this Bill does have considerable support. In fact, this particular clause has support in every country that competes with Canada in the world market for sales of grain, coal, potash, and other bulk commodities. They support the Bill because they know that the imposition of yet another user-fee policy will make Canada and Canadian exports less competitive on the world market. They know that such a policy will make our grains more expensive, that our potash will increase in price, and that it may put some of our producers out of business over the long term. If you like, Mr. Speaker, they welcome a permanent elimination of their competition.
It was with no surprise, Mr. Speaker, that I discovered this particular clause in the Bill. It was clear from this past spring's

October 15, 1985
Canada Shipping Act
federal Budget that the Conservative Government was going to pursue the Liberal Government's cost recovery philosophy. The decision by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to skim $30 million from the assets of the St. Lawrence Seaway Corporation was a clear indication that Seaway tolls would have to rise. I would, however, like to acknowledge and congratulate the Minister of Transportation for having indicated in the House last week that that matter was under review. It is clear that he has an understanding of the needs of the Seaway and the marine industry and is prepared to go to bat for them at the Cabinet level. I encourage him to continue to do so.
I am not surprised that the Government is following the Liberal's philosophy of user-pay. I am, however, disappointed that the Government would bury this clause in this particular Bill, which otherwise, as I mentioned before, is, on the whole, worthy, albeit long overdue, legislation. However, I am not surprised. Although I am surprised that the Minister of Transportation would allow his name to be associated with this particular Bill. When I used to watch Parliament while I was trying to get here I heard the words that the Minister himself used to chastise his predecessor, Otto Lang, on this subject. He said:
Consider the record when it comes to fulfilling the commitments which were made. What has become of those sweeping plans, those radical departures from past methods, those comprehensive programs we heard so much about? What became of the idea of world leadership in transportation? We can probably summarize all this in one phrase: all we have received following these lofty promises amount to nothing more than the Otto Lang user-pay concept.
I go back further into history to June 16, 1958. The Speaker of the House was the then Member of Parliament for Niagara Falls, Mr. W. L. Houck. He was quoting history. Back in 1934, Mr. Speaker, there was a full debate in this House on the motion that all goods shipped through canals owned and operated by the Government of Canada be subject to taxation.
In speaking against the motion, the Hon. R. J. Manion, MP for Fort William from 1917 to 1940-which riding was the predecessor of the riding of Thunder Bay-Atikokan which I now hold-former Leader of the Conservative Party and, at the time, Minister of Railways and Canals, stated in part:
In regard to the Panama, Suez, and Manchester Canals, it is true that they collect tolls. We must realize, however, that the conditions under which these canals are operated are altogether different from those existing in connection with Canadian canals. The Manchester Canal is a private commercial enterprise, whereas in Canada our canals are national. Then the Suez Canal is operated by a privately owned company. True, the Panama Canal is publicly owned and operated, but we must remember this important point: The difference between the Suez, the Panama and our Canadian canals is that no vessel owner is forced to use either the Suez or the Panama.
On the other hand, in Canada we have no alternative water route from the western grain fields, unless one wishes to use the railways from the head of the lakes. As has already been pointed out, however, the railroad would be so much higher that it would not be possible in the marketing of grain. It is important that we should have the lowest possible rates in order that we may compete with countries whose grain fields are closer to the seaboards than are the fields of Canada.
Those words, Mr. Speaker, were no more true in 1933 or 1958 than they are today. In fact, those same words have been echoed by industry spokesmen over the last year as they have warned the Government that it has put the Seaway on the road
to ruin. It is perfectly clear that when we increase transportation costs, whether by increases in fuel costs, taxes, tolls, labour, or materials, those costs ripple through the economy.
The transportation company itself is affected in that it is less able to compete, particularly against other modes, for the movement of, in this case, bulk commodities. The producer, whose products are no longer as competitive in the domestic and foreign market, is directly impacted upon. Due to declining demands for the goods that workers handle, they have less employment and, therefore, less income to spend on consumer goods. Canada as a nation is affected because of a reduction in exports and, therefore, a shift in the balance of payments, because of a reduction in income and corporate tax paid, and because of an increase in the cost of income support programs such as unemployment insurance and welfare that must be paid out to support those laid off workers.
In 1958, the MP for Welland, another riding in this country which has a very direct relationship to marine industry, Mr. W. H. McMillan, said as follows:
As Members of Parliament, we should be interested in the costs of vessel operation in so far as they relate to the cost of moving cargo. We should consider what effect this cost may have on industry generally, on agriculture and commerce. We should be interested in the shipping industry because of the thousands of men who are engaged as seamen and because of the shipbuilders and suppliers, in the same way that we should be interested in the welfare of Canada generally.
I have often read that 40 per cent of our workmen depend for their livelihood on our foreign trade, and I believe that if we are to have a continuing prosperity in this country we must have an expanding trade. The St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes basin, which extends to the very heart of our continent, a distance of 2,900 miles to the sea, are Canada's greatest single outlet to the markets of Europe, the eastern coast of the United States and South America. Much of the trade between Canada and the United States goes across this route. It is the most economical transportation system in the world and, because of its economy, it has helped to build our country. It has helped our farmers to market their wheat in highly competitive markets, even though that wheat is grown thousands of miles from the seaports. It has also helped our industry to assemble raw materials to manufacture products and to enter competitive markets. Today this water transportation system is becoming even more important to the economy of Canada because of the prospective shipping of large tonnages of iron ore from Quebec and Labrador to steel centres along the Great Lakes in both Canada and the United States.
The following also was stated:
One must agree that ultimately tolls are always paid by the consumer, whether he knows it or not. They are included in the cost of transportation and eventually wind up in the price charged for the product. In the case of our basic materials the added cost of transportation through tolls increases in proportion to the number of processes through which the material passes before it finally goes off the dealers' shelves. It is thus cheaper, to say nothing of less painful, for all of us to pay for waterway improvements just once through taxes rather than repeatedly through the higher prices which would result from tolls on the Welland Canal.
That is a final quote from Mr. W. L. Houck, the M.P. for Niagara Falls.
I have a final quote in this series, dated March 12, 1959. It is from a gentleman well known to the House and to you, Mr. Speaker. He is still a Member of Parliament. The then Minister of Transport, the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) said:

October 15, 1985

-this great inland water way will become operative with the opening of the navigation season this year and we have every reason to look forward to the material increase in the volume of shipping using these facilities. This should be of great assistance to the development of the commerce of this country as whole, and should enable goods produced in Canada to become more competitive in world markets. We look forward to the whole economy of Canada benfiting with the opening of this great Seaway project.
Although it is geographically located in the centre of Canada, clearly it is a national asset and should be treated as such. Throughout this debate my colleagues and I will try to put before the House our concerns over the negative impacts of this particular clause. We want to talk about its impact on the commercial fishing industry on the West Coast and the East Coast. We do not believe that those borderline operations can withstand another cost. We want to talk about the impact on recreational boaters as well as the boating industry itself.
Most specifically, we want to deal with its impact on commercial shipping throughout our nation. This will not only hurt the Seaway but will negatively impact on Churchill, Prince Rupert, Vancouver, Saint John, Halifax, Baie Comeau and Port Cartier. Each port and port community in this country will be affected by this Bill. The impact will be severe and nowhere will it be more severe than in the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence system. In fact, I would go so far as to say that when taken in conjunction with other Government action to increase cost recovery, this legislation will kill the Seaway as a viable transportation entity.
In this respect, it is important not to look at the cost recovery measures in this Bill in isolation. We cannot just focus on Clause 4 of Bill C-75; we must look at it in the context of Seaway tolls, Seaway fees and pilotage fees. The Minister knows well, as does his parliamentary assistant, that the industry is howling about the cost increases that they are already facing through the proposed changes to the Laurentian Pilotage Authority as well as their fear that the Minister will not be able to replace the $30 million in the Seaway Authority.
As evidenced by this Bill, it is quite clear that the Government intends to follow this path of cost recovery. Just a few days ago in The Globe and Mail, a paper that is read occasionally by some Members in the House, an aid to the Minister of Transport is quoted as saying:
We're going to make Crown corporations stand on their own two feet.. . The users of the Seaway are going to have to pay most of the cost of the service they get.
Assuming that he was speaking on behalf of the Minister, it is unfortunate that he made such a statement because that kind of approach is not positive for the country and is certainly not positive for the Seaway. This Act gives the Government the power to recover the cost of services that are now provided or will be provided by the Canadian Coast Guard, regardless of whether those services are used by a particular vessel. These services include dredging, ice-breaking, the provision of navigational aids and the provision of ship escort services.
This clause in no way indicates the total extent of that cost recovery. Is it to be 10 per cent, 25 per cent, 50 per cent or even 100 per cent or more? It is my understanding that officials at the Thunder Bay Harbour Commission and offi-
Canada Shipping Act
cials from the Coast Guard have been in negotiation over dredging services for the Port of Thunder Bay all summer. They have been told that the Coast Guard wants to recover 100 per cent of the cost of dredging services within the harbour of the Port of Thunder Bay. Those charges, while levied against the Harbour Commission, will be passed on to the shipper who will pass them on to the producers. Therefore, everyone loses in that cycle.
There are a number of industries whose products are shipped through Thunder Bay and the rest of the Seaway. Their margin is so slim that they are negotiating and competing for pennies and barely able to make anything above the cost of labour. They are competing this way in order to keep in business because they recognize their value not only to the communities where their production originates but to the communities along the Seaway as a result of shipping those goods.
The vast majority of commodities that move through Thunder Bay into the Seaway originate in western Canada. In 1984 alone, 16.6 million tonnes of grain, 2.8 million tonnes of coal and 1.8 million tonnes of potash from as far away as British Columbia was shipped to eastern and foreign markets via Thunder Bay and the Seaway. In fact, in recent years the amount of coal and potash moving through the eastern gate of the Prairies has been on the increase, aided in part by the efficiencies of the Seaway itself. Each year, the Seaway generates $3 billion of economic activity for the ports on both sides of this international waterway.
According to the President of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, Mr. William O'Neil, the Seaway was built, "To serve the grain industry which is now a $6 billion earner of foreign exchange".
Undeniably, the Seaway is uniquely cost efficient for moving transportation intensive bulk products. For less than half the cost of rail, western grain can be loaded on to bulk carriers and shipped from Thunder Bay to eastern ports. Canada's key grain and steel industries demand a low cost bulk system to move their high volume products. The 3,200 kilometres of Seaway is an irreplaceable artery for these industries. Since its completion, the Seaway has moved well over a billion tonnes of cargo. In 1985, the Seaway handled 54 million tonnes through its Welland Canal and 47.4 million through its Montreal-Lake Ontario section. Today, the Port of Thunder Bay ships in excess of 23 million tonnes a year and is responsible for a third of the Seaway's traffic.
According to Robert J. Paterson, Executive Vice-President of NM Paterson and Sons Limited of Thunder Bay, on average, a ship will carry a tonne of cargo 125 per cent farther on a unit of fuel oil than a train, and seven times farther than a truck. Therefore, dollars and cents notwithstanding, in terms of our natural resources it makes more sense to encourage shipments by water.
The head of the grainhandlers in Thunder Bay, Frank Mazur, stated in one of their publications:
We have a world-class seaport on a world-class waterway. Our work force is one of the most productive in the world.
October 15, 1985

Canada Shipping Act
When most Canadians think of grain, they probably think about the infamous Crows Nest Pass rate debate that was held in the House and across the Prairies a few years ago. 1 think the underlying message derived from that debate is that there is a belief in this country that the movement of a commodity like grain must be subsidized because our grain fields are so far from export positions compared to other countries whose ports are 30 miles to 40 miles away. They recognize that we must do something to overcome those obstacles. Perhaps they also recognize that we must ensure that new obstacles are not put into place which prevent products from going to market. Quite honestly, Clause 4 of Bill C-75 puts a very serious obstacle in the way of grain and other bulk commodities being competitive on the world market.
Mr. Donald S. Rothwell, President of the Great Lakes Waterways Development Association, recently said:
The Lakes-Seaway system must get competitive again, in a viciously price conscious world. In an environment where a quarter of a cent per tonne can make a difference, no cost is so insignificant it is inconsequential.
Lower costs are mandatory if traffic is to increase to the point where the Seaway's very stringent cost recovery mandate is to make any economic sense at all. .. Ill-conceived increases in user fees could be counter-productive and result in lower gross revenue to the Government while inflicting serious damage on industries that are already badly wounded by the economic downturn of the early eighties.
The Minister spoke earlier about wanting, once the Bill was passed, to go forth and seek opinions as to what the industry had to say about cost recovery. I respectfully suggest that it should be the other way around. He should have listened to the industry which has been saying for quite some time that it is concerned about the move to cost recovery. Mr. George J. Ryan, President of the Lakes Carriers Association, said:
User charges will wreak havoc on the Great Lakes transportation system and send shock waves through the whole economy. Great Lakes shipping has prevailed through the recession and preserved its assets for better times to come, but user charges could well be the death-knell of this proud industry.
In part, a publication of the Thunder Bay Harbour Commission read:
Excessive tolls have all but driven away the lucrative "general" or "manufactured" cargoes that plied the system in the sixties and seventies. If our Government transfer the costs for Seaway maintenance to the ports, the Seaway will be priced out of business.
Also, Robert J. Paterson from NM Paterson and Sons said:
The user pay cost recovery concept has an obvious political attraction for Government, but its implementation can have severe consequences in efficiency. Fuel surcharges and Seaway user fees pose a serious threat to ship owners and shippers. Private industry is intuitively wary of Government charging back costs when the level of the costs is not subject to the disciplines of the market. We, in the Seaway, are being penalized for being as efficient as we are .. . The Seaway should be treated like every other transportation mode in this country.
If we look at the highways are railroads of our nation, can we really say that they are being charged full cost recovery for their use? I doubt it. I would be very pleased to see a cost comparison, if the Minister happens to have one, showing the various subsidy levels by mode. Then we could take a look at the impact, particularly as it relates to the marine industry. Also Mr. Paterson said:
A greater percentage of the running of the Seaway should be picked up by the general public simply because the Seaway positively affects every citizen of Canada.
During the years of bumper crops in the Prairies or an abundance of grain sales, everyone is happy and everyone is working; grain is moving east, west and north to Churchill. However, during poor years such as last year the inequities or the system become more apparent. The 1984-85 crop was one of the worst in at least six years, if not longer, with a decline of some three million tonnes over previous years. Despite a commitment in the House by the Minister of State For Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), the crop failure was not shared equally throughout the system. For instance, the Port of Prince Rupert saw its throughput decline by 26 per cent; Churchill, by 31 per cent; and Thunder Bay, by 29 per cent. On the other hand, Vancouver was down only 14 per cent over the previous year. While Vancouver was thankfully at full employment last summer, at the Port of Thunder Bay over 1,200 men and women in the grain handling and grain transportation industry were out of work. It was not only in Thunder Bay. Throughout the length of the Seaway, grain handlers and sailors were out of work last summer. The International Seafarers Union estimated that 2,500 of its members were laid off.
If we examine some of the eastern ports downstream, we have a better idea of the trickle effect throughout the country. In two ports in the riding of Manicouagan-and, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you are familiar with the person who represents it- 47.5 per cent of the workforce in the elevators was laid off last summer; in Halifax, 41 per cent; in Saint John, 70 per cent; in Quebec City, 29 per cent; in Trois-Rivieres, 12 per cent; and in Sorel, 60 per cent. Although those percentages are high, the numbers on a broad scale are fairly low. For instance, at Port Cartier, 47 people were laid off and at Baie Comeau 46 people were laid off. Those are smaller communities, and the effect is much greater than in larger centres. Certainly it is important for those 46 and 47 people who were out of work and did not have to be out of work. We estimate that approximately 3,900 people along the Seaway were out of work. When I say "along the Seaway", I am extending it into Manitoba and its rail workers, tradesmen and those at CN shops. People all through the system were out of work because of that inequity. Approximately 51 per cent of the industry was shut down. I suspect- and perhaps the Minister will be able to enlighten us about this later today-that because of the accident, which has shut down the Seaway for a length of time that no one is prepared to estimate, and I can understand the difficulty in doing it, we may see the situation occur again quite quickly where a large number of Canadians are out of work. The trickle down effect is also very severe. It not only affects those people working in the industry, but also those who provide services to them and whose consumer goods they buy.
The American port at Duluth conducted a study a few years ago which found that for every job directly related to the grain industry, there were 2.57 jobs elsewhere in the community. If we look at last summer's unemployment figures, we are talking about 14,000 people who were directly affected by these
October 15, 1985

lay-offs. The cost to UIC alone, if those people were unfortunately laid off for a year, would be $200 million.
At the present time it costs anywher from $23 to $28 per tonne more to move grain through the Seaway to an export position than it does to move it to Vancouver. We are already in a situation where we cannot compete with our western brethren in the Port of Vancouver. The addition of cost recovery measures would in effect be applied unevenly because Vancouver does not have a requirement for ice-breaking whereas Churchill, Thunder Bay and other ports on the Seaway system do. It makes the gap even worse. This is the kind of thing about which I am concerned, as are my colleagues and the industry. This Bill is pushing up that cost.
I have spoken a fair bit about grain and the Port of Thunder Bay, and as well I have touched on some of the ports downstream of Thunder Bay in terms of their unemployment situation this past summer. I should like to continue on that theme for a little longer. Over the summer, Members tend to spend a lot of time in their ridings talking with people, and this past summer I took the opportunity to spend a lot of my time with the people involved in the grain transportation industry. I met with most of the managers of the grain elevators in Thunder Bay and spoke with the managers of the elevators in the eastern part of the system by telephone. As well, I met with the rail superintendents and with the Grain Transportation Authority staff-all in an effort to understand a little more about the movement of grains. And quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I found, on going into it, that my knowledge was very limited. I suspect that most Canadians do not have an appreciation of the nature of the grain industry, both in terms of pricing and competition and how grain moves.
I honestly did not know the relationship between the Port of Thunder Bay and the ten bay ports along the Great Lakes and the Ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres, Baie-Comeau, Port-Car-tier, Halifax, and St. John's. It was through the research that I did this past summer that I was able to get a much better understanding of the system, and I would like to share some of that with you.
As most Members of the House know, when grain or any other bulk commodity moves from western Canada through the St. Lawrence Seaway, it can be picked up by an oceangoing vessel at Thunder Bay-and that is one of the reasons the Seaway was built some 26 years ago-or it can go on a laker for downstream transference to another elevator or directly on to an ocean-going ship.
About 16 per cent of the grain coming through Thunder Bay goes directly on to a "salty." The remainder is distributed throughout the system through the 32 elevators in 18 communities, stretching from Collingwood to Halifax.
For example, 37 per cent of the grain handled in Thunder Bay is handled in the two ports of Manicouagan, Port-Cartier and Baie-Comeau. The ports of Halifax and St. John's handle 2 per cent each; Quebec City, 15 per cent; Trois-Rivieres, 7
Canada Shipping Act
per cent; Sorel, 7 per cent; Montreal, 12 per cent; and then approximately 18 per cent is handled by the ten bay ports.
I said in committee last year that when the West gets sick, Thunder Bay catches pneumonia. Well, if Thunder Bay catches pneumonia, those germs are spread all the way downstream, because the economies of all of the other port commu-nites go up and down with the economy of Thunder Bay.
I mentioned a few moments ago, Mr. Speaker, the competitive aspect. I should like to give the House an idea of what we are up against in the grain industry in terms of competition. This is part and parcel of what we are dealing with, because the higher the fees, the less competitive we will be as a country.
The Manitoba Government conducted a study from 1972 to 1981 comparing the subsidies for grain prevailing in the European Economic Community, the United States and Canada, the three of which, in combination, handled four-fifths of the world's export grain market during that period, a value of (U.S.) $15 billion.
The report produced as a result of that study contained the following statement:
The question at hand is less one of whether in the absence of subsidies everywhere world grain prices would be lower (they would, and so would government expenditures, and hopefully taxes), but rather what is the likely consequence if one grain-exporting nation reduces subsidies unilaterally. Undoubtedly, its grain production and (very likely) exports would decline.
The study group found that, during that 10-year period, our subsidies averaged about 4 per cent, compared to 8.6 per cent in the United States and 10.5 per cent in the EEC. When they examined the year-to-year levels of proportional subsidies, they found a striking difference between Canada and the U.S. On Canadian wheat, for example, subsidies ranged from a low of 2.2 per cent in 1973 to a high of 5 per cent in 1972. In the United States, on the other hand, the variation was much more pronounced, with wheat subsidies as low as 0.8 per cent in 1974 and as high as 22.5 per cent in 1977.
And this clearly reflects the nature of the U.S. grains support programs. U.S. wheat, on average, received $11.41 per tonne in subsidy; Canadian wheat, $6.35; and the EEC, $19.96.
Mr. Speaker, I have the feeling, given the signal you are making, that I am going to have to share my notes with some of my colleagues so that they can continue the arguments in respect of this issue-

along the Seaway. It is crucial to the Port of Churchill and as well to the West Coast ports, particularly the ports of Prince Rupert and Vancouver, and to the maritime ports of Atlantic Canada.

In the light of that, 1 would ask the Minister to reconsider the whole concept. The Minister indicated to the Elouse last week that he would have no objection to the question of the tolls and fees to be charged by the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority being discussed by the Standing Committee on Transport. In that way we can take a good hard look at the whole question of the cost of using the Seaway system and the costs of using our ports. It also will allow us to work with the United States in doing these things in concert.
I should like to hear from the Minister whether or not he has received the agreement of the U.S. officials that they will be moving ahead with their cost recovery in respect of the operation of U.S. ports and whether or not this is a matching duo of operations that we have here, or whether Canada is going on its own in this respect.
And if Canada is going on its own, what is the impact within the St. Lawrence Seaway system? Will a lot more of our bulk commodities go to the United States by rail through Minneapolis and Duluth, or to Chicago? There is already potash going by rail from western Canada to Chicago, instead of coming by rail to Thunder Bay and then by water from Thunder Bay to Chicago.
Mr. Speaker, you as a westerner knows, as do all Members of this House, that we cannot hurt our commodity exports. We are involved in a very vicious fight in world markets.
I should like to conclude by asking the Minister once again to pull Clause 4 out of the Bill. I have been advised that I do not have the ability to move an amendment to have Clause 4 removed from the Bill, and so I would ask the Minister to do so in the interest of maintaining a viable shipping industry in this country.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and Members of the House for your patience.
